Palmer currently is overseeing construction of the $4,150,000 turf and irrigation replacement project at Witter Field, a job expected to last until December. FieldTurf, the synthetic turf which covers the field, had not been replaced in over 16 years, causing drainage issues, rendering Witter into a shallow lake during heavy rains. The new field will utilize a 9-inch deep section of permeable rock below the synthetic turf field and no sand. articles.text: After 17 years of service in Piedmont, City Clerk John Tulloch will end his tenure on Friday, August 4. The City Council declared at its meeting on July 17 that August 4 will be declared John Oliver Tulloch Day. “John’s support has been invaluable as I embark on this journey with the City of Piedmont,” said City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, who was hired in early April. “His devotion to public service and to this community was apparent from our very first meeting,” Moore continued. “Though we’ve worked together only a short time, I will miss his counsel, companionship, and insight. I’m sorry to see him go and wish him the best in future endeavors.” In a discussion with the Post on July 10, Tulloch described his long association with the city in which he grew up. “One of the reasons that I went into government in the first place is because of my experience working with the city as a kid,” said Tulloch, a third-generation Piedmonter. “After being in Schoolmates during my time at Havens and Wildwood, I volunteered in basically every department in Piedmont, particularly working with the Recreation Department in several different jobs,” he said. “When I was five,” he continued, “I would even hang around the fire station to stare at the engines until the firefighters gave me a set of their old gear; I still have it. Under the former Recreation Director Mark Delventhal I worked my first high school job as tennis monitor, where I would supervise the tennis courts on weekends. This community has been a part of me since the very beginning.” Tulloch graduated from Piedmont High School in 1996 and studied at the University of Puget Sound in Tacoma, Washington, earning an undergraduate degree in politics and government in John Tulloch, who has worked in City Hall for 17 years, is leaving his position as City Clerk on Friday, August 4.

articles.text: At their Monday, July 17, meeting, the City Council awarded planning firm JZMK Partners a contract for $588,000 to prepare the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, which provides guidelines for potential implementation of housing in Moraga Canyon. At the meeting, Councilmember Tom Ramsey provided some clarity. The city “is not producing a design … to build something that we’re going to pay for. That’s not what this is. It’s a plan to study the economic and on-site impacts of potential housing in Moraga Canyon,” he said. “This is part of our Housing Element and it’s a requirement of state law. To not do this, we would not be in compliance with state law.” Moraga Canyon Specific Plan JZMK, a Costa Mesa-based firm, will study facets of the Moraga Canyon site including existing land use, utility locations, and topography. The firm will then use this information to create hypothetical housing plans, which will be evaluated for their economic feasibility and effect in Piedmont. After a period of community engagement to determine a preferred plan, JZMK will then create a more detailed site plan, including development standards which will be met for any future housing in Moraga Canyon. One of the key parts of the city’s Housing Element, the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan is intended to plan for potential housing and infrastructure additions on city-owned land in Moraga Canyon, including Blair Park, Coaches Field, Kennelly Skate Park, and the Corporation Yard. The main parts of the plan, which allows two years for implementation, are 132 units of new housing, 60 of which would be lower-income; improved city facilities and recreational open space; improved bicycle, pedestrian, and traffic safety; and wildfire safety measures. Piedmont’s Housing Element, currently in its 6th cycle, outlines proposed policies and programs that would allow the city to accommodate the development of 587 new homes by 2031, a number assigned by the state. This cycle is repeated every eight years. Per state law, “If we chose not to go down this path, we would need to find alternative sites for the units of new housing” than Moraga Canyon, said Planning Director Kevin Jackson. Funding The City Council agenda report for the consultant contract states, “An estimated two- thirds of the [Moraga Canyon Specific Plan] work is anticipated [to be completed] in FY 2023-2024 which amounts to $400,000 in the Approved Budget” from the General Fund for that year. Another $200,000 for the Moraga Canyon will be set aside for the budget in 2024-2025. articles.text: For one week in July, the Piedmont Community Church gym becomes the site of battle for determined young students at a fencing camp operated by Piedmont Fencing Team coach David Sinkkonen has been conducting the summer camp through the Piedmont Recreation Department for 10 years now. The camp held the week of July 10-14, was attended by 18 boys and girls from 3rd through 9th grade, Of the three weapons and associated styles used in fencing – the epee, sabre, and foil – students in the beginning and intermediate-level camps learned to use the most popular, the foil. The students were taught footwork and bladework tactics, en garde drills, and one-on-one matches. Their matches, Sinkkonen explained, were often punctuated with a game somewhere between Lord of the Flies and Capture the Flag, where students with foils are broken into two teams, with one from each team appointed its king or queen. The others, according to their position as guard or knight, are tasked with using their foils to defend or attain territory, marked by orange plastic cones, which surround the other team’s leader. As Sinkkonen plays his preferred soundtrack, “Back in Black” by AC/DC, the gym floods with suited-up youth learning the fine art of fencing – in a whirlwind of controlled chaos. “It’s fantastic seeing the students put the techniques they’ve learned through the drills to the test in engaging, free-for-all games like these,” he said. “It’s a Eighteen students from grades three to nine were enrolled in this year’s summer fencing camp. Staff photos David Sinkkonen has taught fencing in Piedmont and coached the Piedmont Fencing Team for 10 years. fun, win-win dynamic when you combine kids and swords, but it’s always disciplined. We’ve never had any safety problems, as I am super vigilant at all times. “Furthermore,” he continued, “fencing is a very safe sport. For all the years that I’ve been teaching, I’ve never had an accident with anyone being really hurt. For those starting out, I put a lot of emphasis on correct use of the protective masks and jackets before we get into the active play.” A fencer for nearly 50 years, he said that some students from the summer camp go on to join the year-round Piedmont Fencing Team which he coaches. The team has grown from just six members 10 years ago to more than 70 fencers at all skill levels today – an impressive feat for the coach of such an uncommon sport in a small town of 11,000 residents. “For those introduced to fencing through these camps, it takes about three to four years to really gain traction with the sport. The competitive season runs nearly 12 months, from the end of August into July the following year,” he explained. “We’re lucky if we get three weeks off from touring the country” to participate in events like the USA Fencing National Championship, which is held every summer in Phoenix. “This summer camp is a mix between kids interested more in non-competitive activity, primarily learning something new, and those who may be interested in continuing to pursue the sport after the camp is over,” said Sinkkonen. “It’s been difficult building the program for such a non-mainstream sport from scratch in Piedmont, especially given how long it takes to learn the basics. The most rewarding part is seeing how students take to it while they progress here right before you.” Two young fencers in a match on Thursday, July 13

articles.text: Schoolmates registration for the coming 2023-2024 school year opens at 6 p.m. on Wednesday, July 19. Starting this fall, Piedmont Recreation Department’s popular playbased after school care program will have an increased capacity with new, flexible schedule options. This year’s programs offer two choices. “Block Booking” provides a full year of traditional, full afternoon care. Block Booking The Schoolmates “Block Booking” option offers predetermined time slots for families needing consistent weekly care throughout the year: • Register once for the full school year (program runs September 5 to May 24) • Sign up by day of the week for full afternoon care (3-6 p.m. most weekdays, 1:45-6 p.m. on Wednesdays) • Waitlist available Tuition for Schoolmates Block Booking is $11.20/hour, billed monthly. Flexi-Care The new Schoolmates “FlexiCare” program offers registration in hourly increments, allowing families to select only the days and times they need: • Separate enrollment periods for fall (September 5 to December 21) and spring (January 8 to May 24) • Option to adjust schedule monthly, pending availability • No waitlist Tuition for Schoolmates FlexiCare is $13.40/hour, billed monthly. Camp Kaleidoscope Another new offering this year, Camp Kaleidoscope, provides expanded care during the first few weeks of school, when demand is the highest. Camp Kaleidoscope offers weekly flexibility and a rotation of fun enrichment activities ranging from sports and scavenger hunts to cooking and arts & crafts. Camp Kaleidoscope runs from 2 to 6 p.m., August 14 to September 1. Spots are available at the Beach School and Havens School locations. Minimates The Minimates program offers Piedmont students in transitional kindergarten opportunities to learn, grow, and have fun with age-appropriate games, crafts, and sports. • Register once for the full school year (program runs August 14 to May 24) • Sign up by day of the week for full morning (8:30 a.m. class start) or full afternoon (class release at 3 p.m.) • Waitlist available Tuition for Minimates is $11.20/ hour, billed monthly. articles.text: Piedmont Middle School’s Annie Holland retired at the end of the school year after teaching for 24 years in the district. Holland started in 1999 as a 7th grade core teacher and became the history teacher at the middle school. Her career was honored at the May 24 school board meeting by colleagues and community members. Holland expressed her gratitude for the Piedmont community as well. “It’s been 24 years that went by in a blink of an eye, even longer since our first son started kindergarten 37 years ago. It’s going to be the first fall without some buttress of the district holding us up,” Holland said. Each board member took time to thank Holland, as did teachers’ union president Elise Marks. “A student once told me ‘we will always be kind to Ms. Holland because she is always kind to us.’” said PMS Principal Karyn Shipp. Holland thanked her husband Bill whom she met in the third grade. “I could never have taught distance learning without Bill honestly. I did not know enough about computers. I was weeping, saying ‘what am I going to do,’ Piedmont Middle School history teacher Annie Holland retired in June this year. but he was right there and fixed everything,” said Holland. “Both of our kids remember you so fondly,” said board member Hilary Cooper. “You are the kind of teacher that a parent hopes their kids will have.” Holland looks forward to being kept busy in retirement by spending time with her seven grandchildren. “My mother was also a teacher and her advice that I always have in my mind is ‘treat your students the way you would want a teacher to treat your own children or grandchildren.’ That has been a guiding principle,” said Holland.

articles.text: Chabot Space & Science Center will present its annual BubbleFest event this Saturday and Sunday, July 22-23 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Now a two-day event, BubbleFest explores the wonders of the remarkable spheres we know as bubbles. BubbleFest will bring together learners of all ages to learn about bubble physics and how bubbles can teach us about star formation and all its applications in space science. BubbleFest is geared towards a family audience but welcomes all visitors to celebrate the joy of bubbles with hands on bubble fun, music, and the experience of being inside a giant bubble. Returning this year are bubble artists Tom Noddy and Sterling Johnson. Johnson will create beautiful, large bubbles with found objects. Kids can experience the wonder of Tom Noddy’s Bubble Magic as well. Participants are encouraged to join the whirlwind of fun, playing in our outdoor bubble play area and making bubbles out of everyday objects. Non-member tickets are Adults: $20, Children (2-12): $15, Seniors (65+): $10 History of Chabot Chabot Space & Science Center is a non-profit institution and community resource located on 13 trail-laced acres in Redwood Regional Park in Oakland amid the largest stand of coastal redwoods in the East Bay. Chabot features a 241-seat full dome planetarium, interactive and hands-on exhibits, space artifacts, a giant screen theater, NASA Ames Visitor Center, and the only research-level telescopes regularly available to the public for weekly live viewing in the Western United States. Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the Universe and Planet Earth. Located at 10000 Skyline Blvd. in Oakland, Chabot Space & Science Center is open Wed.- Sun. 10 am-5 pm with First Fridays the first Friday of every month 6-10 pm.

articles.text: As part of a new Free Children’s Book Day program, kids aged 12 and under can take home a free children’s book of their choice on the second Sunday of every month at The Bookmark Bookstore in Old Oakland. Laura Guzman, who co-manages The Bookmark with Sven Geddes, said that the program began on June 11, and recently held its second Free Book Day on July 9. The event is run by the nonprofit Friends of the Oakland Public Library (FOPL), which manages the bookstore. “Each time so far, we’ve had about 20 families with children coming in,” said Guzman. “As there were a few repeats at the second event, we’re hoping to build a crowd month by month. Because all of our books are donated, the selection is very eclectic. Most books in the store have been published within the last 10 years, although children’s books tend to have a longer life due to the generally perennial subjects they deal with.” “We had talked about the free book program with the library about two to three months before it began, so they could start getting the word out in the community,” said Geddes. “That first time in June the kids were so excited to come in that we had three families waiting outside the store 15 minutes before we opened. That’s been the best part – seeing that the program is so kid-driven. They’re the ones who want to come in and who are overjoyed to be getting a book,” said Geddes. “The library is an invaluable resource, but it’s also crucial for any kid to grow up with books available in their own home to grab and read.” The Bookmark recently received a staggering donation from Bibliomania, a bookstore in Oakland which closed their brickand-mortar location on Telegraph Avenue to operate online. They donated nearly 3,000 children’s picture books, mostly published in the 1970s and ‘80s and all in excellent shape. “For children’s books, our inventory is completely updated every month. Books sit on our shelves for about four months maximum, and if they don’t sell by then, we give them a new life and send them out to another Friends public library system or to a nonprofit, like the Prisoners Literature Project in Berkeley,” said Guzman. “Nothing’s stale - it’s fun to come back to the store. What you’ll find is different every time.” “Not only are children’s books free every second Sunday,” added Geddes, “but we’re still the cheapest used bookstore around. We’re proud that the proceeds all go back to the community.” Other than Guzman and Geddes, the children’s book program and the bookstore itself are run entirely by a pool of approximately 50 volunteers, working three to four people at a time across three shifts a day to help sort, shelve, process, and sell donated books on- and off-site. More information about Friends of Oakland Public Library is available at fopl.org. The next Free Children’s Book Day event will take place at The Bookmark on Sunday, August 13. articles.text: If you are in the North Lake Tahoe area, take a worthy side trip to Washeshu Peak for a million-dollar view while hiking at an elevation of 8,000 feet. As of July 2023, there are still patches of snow, but hikers can cross it using hiking shoes. Palisades Tahoe Olympic Valley – the former Squaw Valley – is a popular destination for Piedmont residents, especially during Ski Week in February. But during the summer months, the region becomes a prime hiking location with wildflowers and sweeping awe striking views of Lake Tahoe and Desolation Wilderness. Washeshu is in commemoration of the Washoe Tribe. Early literature from the tribe indicates the term Wa She Shu translates to “People from here.” Our day starts by taking the aerial tram ride up to High Camp, which gives another incredible view from the viewing platform back towards Lake Tahoe, a popular restaurant, outdoor games, a skating rink, and Olympic museum dedicated to the 1960 Winter Games. The large-scale pool and hot tub, unfortunately, has remained closed for several years due to extensive repairs. From High Camp, walking to Washeshu Peak is a two-mile straight shot and around 850 feet in elevation gain with the final 0.6 of a mile to the peak provides the sharpest ascent. The trail averages less than 10 percent gradient for the first 1.3 miles before making the climb to Washeshu Peak. At the 1.3 mile mark, hikers will come to a junction with a path on the left shooting upwards towards the Siberia Express ski lift, while the preferred trail on the right going takes you along the back-end toward Washeshu Peak. articles.text: The Piedmont Fencing Team just wrapped up its season at the prestigious National Championships in Phoenix from June 30 – July 9, where 5,300 athletes from 43 states came to compete. Piedmont Fencing Team sent seven athletes to this year’s event, including five current Piedmont residents. Representing the program were Piedmont High juniors Teresa McKay and Oliver Greenebaum, sophomores Jonah Kim and Niko Kalamas, and Piedmont Middle School 8th grader Dario Banuelos. Tamalpais senior Lorenz Finney also competed, and Sophie Choi, who moved from Piedmont to Danville, also competed at the Y-12 level. It’s a remarkable achievement considering the program had under 10 members when coach David Sinkkonen took over a decade ago to now 70 while training at the Piedmont Community Church. “The National Championships are hard and everyone had a great time. It’s an achievement to even make it to National Championships and all of it is coming out of the community church [where the team practices]. When I think of it that way, it’s pretty incredible,” said coach David Sinkkonen. At National Championships, Kim competed in five events. He was 46th of 203 in the Division 3 men’s foil category, 92nd of 302 in the Y-14 men’s foil, finished 151st of 220 in the Division 2 men’s foil, was 216th of 344 in the junior men’s foil, and 254th of 269 in the cadet U-16 men’s foil. Jonah Kim competed in five events at the National Championships. The Piedmont Fencing Team sent seven members to the National Championships in Phoenix from June 30 to July 9. Pictured are PHS junior Oliver Greenebaum (left), PHS sophomore Jonah Kim, PHS junior Teresa McKay, Tamalpais senior Lorenz Finney, and coach David Sinkkonen. “Jonah fenced in five events; he was there the whole time. He made it out of the preliminary rounds in each event, but couldn’t get traction after that… I feel really good about his development. He’s definitely going places,” said Sinkkonen. Greenebaum was also busy, competing in three events. He placed 108th in the D3 men’s foil category, 162nd in the cadet men’s foil, and 336th in the junior men’s foil. Niko Kalamas, meanwhile, was 300th in the junior men’s foil. McKay was in the cadet U-16 women’s foil category, finishing 126th of 212. In the Y-12 category was Banuelos finishing 220nd. “For Teresa and Niko, it was their first National Championships. Teresa made it out of the preliminary round. articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony will perform at Stern Grove Festival on July 23. The Symphony is a recurring guest of the festival every year. Stern Grove Festival is a series of ten summer concerts, held on Sundays from June 18 through August 20 at a natural amphitheater in San Francisco surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees. The grove’s natural acoustics have been preserved as a park in which the public could enjoy admission-free music, dance, and theatre performances. Stern Grove Festival has brought 80 years of a diverse range of performing arts to the City. The Symphony will be joined by special musical guest Lettuce, a Boston-based funk band that formed in 1992. Its members are guitarist Adam “Shmeeans” Smirnoff, Nigel Hall (keyboards, Hammond B-3 organ, piano, vocals), Adam Deitch(drums/percussion), Erick “Jesus” Coomes (bass), Ryan Zoidis (saxophone) and Eric “Benny” Bloom (trumpet). The band has gained a cult following in major cities and released their newest album Unify last year. The event is free but reservation is required and space is limited. Visit https://www.sterngrove.org to reserve your spot. San Francisco Symphony cellists shown in a 2019 concert at Stern Grove

The performance on July 27, entitled “Points of View,” features professional staging, lights, costumes, and live music. It is free and open to the public. “AileyCamp gives young people an opportunity to have a quality arts experience, make friends, express themselves, and recognize that they matter,” said Nasha Thomas, AileyCamp National Director. “Every year, it is a joy to witness the campers’ transformation from the first day to the final performance. It’s incredibly special to watch our former campers step into leadership roles that pay it forward to the next generation. It’s a testament to Alvin Ailey’s mission of enriching the lives of youth through dance.” For more information and tickets, visit Cal Performances’ website at www.calperformances.org/ aileycamp.

articles.text: Blues musician Henry St. Claire Fredericks Jr., better known by his stage name Taj Mahal, will perform at Miner Auditorium at SF Jazz in San Francisco August 3 through 6. Blues legend Taj Mahal plays a plethora of instruments including the guitar, piano, banjo, and harmonica. His 50-year career spans several genres that blend sounds from the Caribbean, Africa, India, Hawaii and the South Pacific. Originally from Harlem in New York City, Fredericks began his music career after moving to Los Angeles in 1964 where he formed the band Rising Sons with fellow blues rock musicians. He has performed at venues throughout the Bay Area, including at Stern Grove Festival last year. The blues icon returns to Miner Auditorium with a tribute to the legendary Harlem swing music of the 1930’s and 40’s. The performances, hosted by SF JAZZ, will feature folk singer Blues musician Taj Mahal Maria Muldaur and will include an orchestra. All shows August 3 through 6 begin at 7 p.m. Miner Auditorium is located at 201 Franklin Street in San Francisco. articles.text: Visit the Treasure Island Museum this Saturday, July 22, to view the museum’s newest exhibition “Treasure Island: Inspiring Artists Since 1939.” Treasure Island Museum is a nonprofit that preserves the island’s little-known, Pacific-themed heritage. The program this Saturday focuses on the 1939 Golden Gate International Exposition, where hundreds of artists were commissioned to create sculptures and murals for the island’s buildings and gardens. Almost all signs of the World Fair are gone, but since the museum’s creation in 1975 the City of San Francisco has made earnest efforts to preserve the island’s rich history. Color photography emerged during this time to capture and preserve the legacy of the Golden Gate International Exposition. The program will include how this history inspires contemporary and modern, local artists. Katy Boynton and Tom Loughlin are artists who use materials and ideas from the past to create new public art on and off Treasure Island. The exhibition program will be presented by museum board member and historian Anne Schnoebelen, and artists Boynton and Loughlin. The program begins at 10:30 a.m. Tickets are $10. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.treasureislandmuseum.org/event-details/treasure-island-inspiring-artists-since-1939-3. Treasure Island Museum General Dentistry & Advanced Prosthodontics

articles.text: Eddie Redmayne and Alicia Vikander in The Danish Girl It’s 1926 in Copenhagen, Denmark. Two artists, Einar Wegener (Eddie Redmayne) and his wife, Gerda (Alicia Vikander), married some six years, live a contented, Bohemian life, both in search of galleries that will carry their work. Einar, a landscape painter, is finding more success than Gerda, who has thus far confined herself to portraits of wealthy burghers. Their connection, through touch and gaze, reflects a sustained intimacy, revealing in countless subtle ways a relationship that they both cherish as they stand before easels, working, or waking in the early morning, basking in the soft early morning light, the diaphanous curtains of the bedroom creating a luminescent glow. Looking out the woodframed windows of their starkly furnished flat is a harbor filled with working boats, their cinnabar and white sails raised, swaying ever so slightly in the wind. The Danish Girl is replete with achingly gorgeous moments, not only between Einar and Gerda, but horizons framed by pink sunsets and bucolic hills obscured by orange and red wildflowers, each image suffused with color and beauty. Together they share life’s continuum, a kaleidoscope of small and not so small changes. But the depth and breath of their marriage, a touching and visible bond, is seemingly inviolable. What they are unprepared for is the change that Einar will embark on, a journey that will take him into the distance where his once very masculine image begins to fade until it is barely visible, as if he were standing behind a scrim, his outline growing increasingly dim. What Gerda is unprepared for is what she set in motion, simply on a lark. She initially asks Einar to pose, covered by a formal gown, her intention only to finish a portrait; she needed the lower legs and feet completed. Einar’s reaction to the feel of the dress, the sheer hose covering his calves, catches him by surprise, stirring emotions that both surprise and disturb. Gerda is oblivious, her focus on the painting. And so begins for them both a long and unsettling goodbye, defined by anguish and love and an unflinching commitment. Einar is headed into the unknown, to a point on the far end of the spectrum of change. To look at Gerda, her face lovely to behold, even when broken by a wrenching agony, is to find Einar’s choice seemingly inexplicable. And yet to be human, fully human, is to engage in what can be a lifelong quest for self – to be fully oneself. If that is a truism, then it gradually becomes clear that Einar feels incarcerated, often against his will in a body he does not feel is his own. Gerda, however, cannot initially, begin to comprehend what is made manifest. The Danish Girl is breathtaking. It is wondrous in so many ways, not the least of which are the portrayals of Eddie Redmayne and Alicia Vikander. They completely inhabit their characters. And it is not just Redmayne who must make an astonishing transformation to Lili Elbe. Vikander must summon a depth of understanding and loyalty that encases her in a steely resolve that is for her also a precipice. There are images of each of them in which their eyes convey a sense of torment and loss that they are both powerless to change. The heartbreaking arc of their lives has been set. Keep in mind that in 1926 what Einar was moving toward was the breaking of a taboo for which there was no name, other than schizophrenia. He could only look to Gerda, pleadingly, hopelessly, while she reassured him that he was not mentally deranged or confused. He simply was. She was remarkable. As is this deeply human and moving film. The Danish Girl. Directed by Tom Hooper. Starring Eddie Redmayne, Alicia Vikander and Ben Whishaw. 120 min., Rated R. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv

Some artists are overlooked, despite an abundance of legitimate talent. Gregory Taboloff might be included in the short list. His concert on Saturday evening proved this. As a pianist, he has a tone somewhat like the immortal Arthur Rubinstein. It is rich and resonant, fortified by clean articulation and intelligent musicianship… all put to the service of the music. The format of Taboloff’s concert was something like a good music appreciation program. The spoken program notes increased the audience’s appreciation. That’s how music education should be. articles.text: For the first time in 43 years the actors’ union, Screen Actors Guild – American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA) joined the Writers Guild of America on the picket line, bringing the $134 billion American movie and television business to a halt. One of the unresolved issues is, of course, pay; however, keep in mind that there are a combined 170,000 members of The Writers Guild and SAG who want to make what they refer to as a living wage. What makes this strike unique is that both groups added to their contract negotiations/demands the inclusion of new guidelines that address the fast-changing technology now being utilized not only in moviemaking, such as A.I. (artificial intelligence), but also digitally altering actors’ images as well as scripts absent any residual payments (royalties). And there is also the impact on the industry of streaming. I would add to the analysis of the strike the effects on the overall industry of the recent and long-lasting COVID pandemic, which indisputably altered the movie-going experience resulting in countless empty theaters. Thus far we are finding that there is a slow and tenuous return of what was a once robust audience. The advent of streaming platforms such as Netflix, Prime, Paramount+, and Apple tv, combined with home entertainment screens offering unparalleled size and clarity. have been revolutionary. The drop in industry revenues and box office earnings have resulted in layoffs by the studios, to include the effects on adjunct businesses such as background actors, grips, techies, and even catering companies who will soon begin feeling the impact of lost business. The question now is how long will the strike last? The writers have already been out more than 70 days and neither the studios – Disney, Sony, Universal, Paramount – or the unions have shown a willingness to return to the bargaining table. At this point there is no red carpet that leads to a comprehensive solution.
articles.title: GUEST ESSAY Deciphering the Hollywood Actors and Writers strike

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré The Longest Ride is the 10th film adaptation of a Nicholas Sparks novel. If you’ve read or seen The Notebook, this film will seem very familiar. But then Sparks is a master at recycling his plots by merely changing the context and rarely the content. He’s a master of the formulaic love story, and The Longest Ride is no exception. Two young people from different worlds meet cute at a rodeo., Luke Collins (Scott Eastwood) is a champion bull rider, and Sophia (Britt Robertsons) is a college senior at Wake Forest, majoring in art, preparing to accept an internship at a major New York gallery. They manage to arrange a first date, have an idyllic picnic by a lake, and on their way home spot a traffic accident. articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Your Name is a remarkable coming-of-age story, written and directed by the Japanese animator and storyteller Makoto Shinakai who is considered the next Hayao Miyazaki (Spirited Away), founder of Ghibli Sudios. In 2017, Your Name it was one of Japan’s highest grossing anime films and eventually was embraced by most of Asia. This beautifully rendered film (using hand-drawn and CGI animation), set in 2013, focuses on two teenagers, Taki Tachibana (Michael Sinternikiaas) and Mitsuha Miyaamzu (Stephanie Shen). Both are in high school. Taki lives in urban Tokyo and Mitsuha in a rural village, a place she finds missing even a hint of excitement. In other words, she is a restless, bored teen. And then the extraordinary happens. One morning the two wake up and discover that though they don’t know each other, they have swapped bodies and soon come to realize that each must now go through the other’s day at school while grappling with this unexpected, confusing occurrence. Your Name is a tale that centers on perspective, asking how their lives will change regarding their daily activities and old friendships. Mitsuha becomes more popular and gregarious. Taki seems more withdrawn. The teens soon figure out how to communicate, leaving notes and calls, (even messages on each other’s skin); however, they never actually meet. As you might guess, their connection gradually deepens and they begin to have a crush on each other. And so Your Name morphs into a teen romance. The story also unexpectedly becomes one touching on time travel, disasters, a ghost story, and a comedy of errors, and reveals itself to be a meditation on identity and connection. As an aside the artwork is stunning, and, of course, there are the signature eyes that are extraordinary while asking the question, to what degree are we defined by our appearance. Your Name. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s 2nd Thursdays Flix Fest had its July showing on July 13 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts and featured a classic. Some movie directors — very few — are as famous as the actors whose performances they shape: Orson Welles, Alfred Hitchcock and Steven Spielberg are among them, and Stanley Kubrick is in that company, for helming a series of iconic films: Spartacus, Lolita, Dr. Strangelove, 2001, A Clockwork Orange, and The Shining. All movie careers begin somewhere, and though Kubrick had directed a couple of previous films, his first notable work is 1956’s stark, taut The Killing, which Piedmonters had a chance to see at last week’s Thursday Film Fest in the Center for the Arts. Filmed nearby in San Mateo and at Bay Meadows Racetrack, the film was written by Kubrick and Jim Thompson and photographed in pungent black and white by cinematographer Lucien Ballard. It’s set in seedy hotel rooms but mostly at that racetrack, which in the story has two million in cash in its safe, just waiting to be boosted. Career criminal Johnny Clay (an edgy Sterling Hayden) is the chief booster, recruiting a sharpshooter, a crooked policeman, a bartender, and a betting teller to help him complete the heist. He’s got a soft spot, though – all he wants to do is retire with his innocent fiancée, Fay, played by a tremulous Colleen Gray. Needless to say, as in all noir films, Fate comes to call, and it’s not a Fate that looks kindly on Johnny Clay, who ends watching all that stolen cash fly away on the wind. The Piedmont screening was introduced by Mike Gallant who after the movie led a discussion with the attendees. Their reactions to the movie were very positive. They enjoyed this view back in time to the 1950s and the start of Kubrick’s career. The movie brought back memories of the classic Dragnet television series of that time. Just like it, The Killing was filmed in black & white, and it would not have been right to do it any other way. The music might be a little overly dramatic by today’s standards, but the viewers enjoyed Kubrick’s use of multiple story lines to tie the different characters’ actions together. It was noted that Kubrick was originally a photographer for Life magazine, which may have influenced the look of his film. Viewers were taken aback by the use of a disparaging racial slur by a bad guy, and wondered how it was received at the time. Those attuned to the subtleties of Kubrick’s fun style noted that one of the racehorses was named “Stanley K.” Everyone agreed this and The Killing were fun. Coming next in the movie series on August 10th is the Italian comedy, Pranzo di Farragusto (Lunch in August). Sponsored by the Piedmont Recreation Department, the Flix Fest takes place in the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with a show time at 10:30. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration with the PRD is required at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Guests are welcome to bring snacks or lunch.

articles.text: The First Mondays Reading Group had a strong turnout of 19 readers on July 10 for a discussion of How Beautiful We Were by Cameroonian-American novelist Imbolo Mbue. This novel was inspired by Mbue’s own experiences growing up in Cameroon. It is an environment-themed novel set in a fictional village of Kosawa in Africa, in the 1980s. The story follows a set of villagers who challenge their government and an American oil company. The people are angered by the firm, Pexton, which causes oil spills and fatal illnesses. A villager, Kanga, convinces the villagers to revolt. However, they are repressed by the corrupt president of their country. There is a revolution by the young adults led by a woman named Thula. She has grown up in the village and has experienced the harm Pexton’s pollution has caused her people. She is talented and wins scholarships and to a college in the United States. She develops a relationship with a young American and has the potential for a bright future, but she gives it all up to forge a militant organization to protest against Pexton and her government. Sadly it does not end well for the people. How Beautiful We Were received mixed, but on the whole, positive reviews from the readers. They benefited from the view into this world that the book provided. It was an “eye opener” for some readers regarding the destructive colonialism that exists in parts of the world today. The book provided an understanding of the harm that can be caused by bad governments and exploitive corporations from the victims’ perspectives. Children are dying because of the pollution and government soldiers kill the people too. These are gentle people who are dragged down by one hurtful thing after another. The readers hoped something good would happen to them, but it doesn’t. The book’s ending was liked best by some, but it was still a sad story. Readers could relate to the personal experience stories of abuse, corruption, and injustice. They recognized the same type of environmental exploitation is happening around the world and in parts of the United States too. Leaking, capped oil and gas wells in our South, with their harmful effects on the land and people, were considered. Readers felt we have a responsibility for what is happening abroad and at home, but there are no good answers for what to do about it. So, there was also a feeling of guilt by some readers. How Beautiful We Were is thought-provoking and it generated some conversations on: Should individuals contest powers that are not aligned with their values, and if so, how? Can working within a system that you don’t agree with result in greater good than fighting it? What should we teach our children and what can they teach us? The questions made How Beautiful We Were a worthwhile read. How Beautiful We Were by Imbolo Mbue was the July book for discussion. The readers had previously selected Four Fish: The Future of the Last Wild Food by Paul Greenberg for their August read. There were a number of good suggestions for future books. The group decided on A Visit from the Goon Squad by American author Jennifer Egan for September, The Life and Times of the Thunderbolt Kid by Bill Bryson for October, The Trees by Percival Everett for November, and The Finest Hours by Michael J. Tougias and Casey Sherman for December. The group’s next discussion will be on August 7 at 1:30 p.m. outside the Tea House by the Community Hall. New readers are welcome to join the group and there is no fee, Registration is required at https://bit.ly/3R86PP4. articles.text: It is with heavy hearts that the Lambing family announces the passing of our mother, long time Piedmont resident Pat Lambing. In recent years she lived in Walnut Creek, and then moved to Reno, Nevada, to be closer to family. Pat attended Bishop O’Dowd High School, and then matriculated at Holy Names College where she attained a degree in Speech Pathology and Audiology. She met Dr. Robert Lambing on a blind date, and six months later, they were married – a marriage that lasted for 41 years. She put her degree and possible career aside to raise four children who all attended Piedmont schools. Susan Lambing of Puyallup, WA, Linda (Dee-Dee) Lambing, deceased in 1983, Dr Robert Lambing of Monterey, CA, and Patricia Lambing Nishkian of Reno, NV. Pat was always involved in the greater good, serving as the past president of the Alameda County Cancer League, Easter Pat Lambing Seals Society, Junior League of the East Bay, Mothers Against Drunk Driving, Piedmont Boy Scouts and countless other volunteer positions throughout her life. She had an amazing ability to nurture and love children, which she enjoyed immensely. She was a classy and graceful woman, with an epic sense of style. We all find solace knowing that she is reunited with her beloved husband Bob, and her adored daughter Dee-Dee in God’s Kingdom.

articles.text: Sharon Ho started her career as an RN at Children’s Hospital in 1980. The Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) was in its nascent stage and she had the incredible opportunity to witness firsthand the wonderful work done by the dedicated nursing and medical staff in the NICU. She found the work gratifying and challenging at the same time as she witnessed the immense dedication of the staff. To this end, the nursing staff was ever present to lend support and their expertise to these families in need. One of Sharon’s real estate colleagues, Mavis Delacroix holds a special place in her heart for Children’s Hospital as well. Her eldest son was in a near fatal car accident when he was brought to Oakland’s Children’s Hospital by ambulance. After more than five hours in surgery and several weeks in the hospital, the entire family celebrated when he was able to return home. Mavis and her family were impressed with the expert level of care and compassion her son received from the surgeon to the house keeping staff. Their shared personal connections to the hospital is what brought this idea together. It has been a privilege to witness the compassion, dedication of the hospital team, who work tirelessly to improve the lives of children and their families. They wanted to express gratitude and show support for the foundation’s invaluable efforts. Together they made the decision to organize a fundraiser at a newly renovated home in Piedmont where handcrafted cocktails and light bites were served. articles.text: – Joseph Campbell As seniors get older, they may face many challenges in life. Loss of health or loved ones can affect them deeply. While life is filled with ups and downs for all of us and we will not be happy at every moment, it is important to try and help seniors when they are experiencing sadness. Caregivers can play a crucial role in spreading joy to those in their care. Here are four ideas to assist you in bringing happiness to a senior. take to help fill their time with enjoyable activities. Here is a list of a few that they can try: Activities for Seniors • Yoga. There are many yoga classes designed specifically for seniors. Yoga can help calm the mind and body, especially yoga exercises that are slow and gentle. Seniors with limited mobility can try doing chair yoga which will allow them to increase strength, flexibility and breath awareness, all from a seated position. • Painting. Art is an excellent form of self-expression and a great outlet for seniors to share their experiences with the world. Studies have shown that art therapy has many benefits, both physical and mental, for seniors. Picking up a paintbrush can help seniors keep their motor skills sharp and improve hand-eye coordination. The bright, vibrant colors can boost their mood and help reduce depression or anxiety. Painting can also assist seniors with concentration skills and memory, all while improving confidence and giving them a sense of control. • Cooking. There are many cooking classes geared towards seniors which may offer advice regarding specific diets, such as making nutritious meals or meals with low salt content. These classes can be taken in-person which allows seniors to make social connections and establish friendships. Or, for the senior who has a hard time getting out or who prefers to take classes from the comfort of home, there are online options as well. Treat them with compassion. When interacting with parents, grandparents and other loved ones, it’s important to remember to speak with compassion. Seniors want to know that their voice matters and that they will be treated with dignity. We should strive to always speak to seniors with care, patience, and respect, being mindful of any physical or mental challenges they are experiencing. If you can do this, you will see that your efforts go a long way in bringing joy to seniors and making them feel appreciated. Homewatch CareGivers is located at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmonters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com. Encourage the use of assistive devices to maximize independence. As people age, they may become less mobile and experience difficulty performing daily tasks. They might not know how to ask for help but there are many products they can use to make their life simpler and more comfortable. Reach out to your healthcare provider for a PT/OT consultation to ensure that you are using the correct devices for your particular needs. If your senior loved one is having a hard time walking, they can use a scooter or walker to help them get around. It may also be helpful to have a shower seat or grab-bars installed in their bathroom, to assist them in safely moving around the room. Seniors experiencing dexterity issues can also utilize products to make their life easier, such as an electric toothbrush. Ask for their stories. Just like all of us, older adults want to know that their life has meaning. Ask them to tell you about one of their favorite memories – for example, “What did you enjoy doing most as a kid?” “Did you have a favorite pet when you were growing up?” “What has brought you the most joy in life?” It’s important to listen closely and ask relevant questions as they share details from their life. Many seniors feel like no one remembers them or that they are a burden to their loved ones. You can counteract these feelings by asking to know more about them and their past. articles.text: Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: My wife and I just updated our will and trust, but I feel like I should make other preparations. For example, should I give my passwords to my kids, so they can access my computer when I pass away? -Allen P., Oakland Dear Allen: The more that you can prepare your family members for the event of your passing, the easier time they will have with the immense work involved in settling an estate. I know that most of us work hard to make sure we have all our financial affairs in order so our beneficiaries will have an easier time when we pass, but there are so many things in our digital life that we don’t think of. One of my nephews, who works in cyber security says that each person should create a digital “If I Go Missing” folder that contains all our important passwords and phone numbers. Things like our email passwords, credit card and bank passwords, airlines, shopping and Apple ID to name a few. If you just examine your daily routine, you will be amazed at how many times you must sign in or authenticate to access an account, a website, a subscription or your bank. It’s a good idea to take notes for a week or so, to determine what to add to this folder or document. Now comes the tricky part. If you have a document or a spreadsheet with all this vital information, where can you keep it securely and away from hackers or thieves? Here are a few possibilities: 1. On a piece of paper in a safe. As long as you give the combination to your home safe and let your family members know that this document is there, it’s as safe as anything in your home. Which is to say, it can be stolen or broken into, but still better than in a drawer in your desk. 2. A document on your computer. This is the most common solution and can be encrypted with a password. Again, you must let your family members know how to get into your computer and where this document is stored. But this is not the best solution, as it’s not very secure and often difficult to access when you are not present.

articles.text: Shortly after 4 a.m. on Sunday morning, July 9, suspects in three vehicles drove to the side door of Ace Hardware on Grand Avenue, disabled the alarm and made entry into the store. After two sessions of ransacking the store, the suspects stole an estimated $100,000 in merchandise and money. Based upon surveillance photos, after one ten-minute session ransacking the business for valuable merchandise, the suspects left, and briefly parked at Safeway. When no alarm or alert was heard, they returned to enter the building again to the back of the building and spent 25 minutes stealing items. According to Ace Hardware Manager Shaun Braga it was the second stint of burglary that resulted in the biggest loses. Power tools and cash were taken, and items were strewn all around the store and parking lot. A door on the side of the building was pried open and bolt cutters were used to cut a padlock. Piedmont police found the bolt cutter left behind. Surveillance video showed one of the three suspect vehicles leaving the city two hours later, at 6:17 a.m. Police Dispatch was notified of the loss at 8:40 a.m. Grand Ace Hardware, which has been in business for 50 years, has hired a security guard since the robbery.

This variety in different tasks that I’ve been responsible for during my time with the city has always kept me fascinated, alongside my love of the community I get to work with.” “My time in City Hall has shown me that where Piedmont works best is where the community comes together — take Hampton Field, or the pool project,” he continued. “When I came into City Hall, even as a kid, I was always taken seriously. I walked in with a question, an idea and I got an answer, a response. And I’ve really been proud of continuing that for community members of any age who come in with a question,” he continued. “John has been an indispensable member of our small City team,” said Vice-Mayor Betsy Andersen. “Throughout City Hall he’s admired for his unparalleled knowledge of Piedmont history, unmatched expertise in all things elections, and unwavering commitment to delivering high-quality, good government core services. But for me, what has always stood out the most about John is his dedication to putting the community first. In this, he sets a remarkable benchmark for us all to aspire to. He will truly be missed.” Why, then, depart from City Hall now, Tulloch was asked. “It’s something I’ve been thinking about for a while,” Tulloch said. “I think that the City Council made a fantastic decision in hiring Rosanna Bayon Moore as City Administrator; she comes with a wealth of knowledge and experience. When Sara Lillevand, the former City Administrator, announced that she was going to leave, I wanted to remain here long enough to get Rosanna on her feet before I decided to go on. It’ll be four months since she started, when I leave.” He will not immediately be looking for another job and will use the time to decompress from the 23 years he has been working since graduating from college. Tulloch said that he is looking forward to spending more time with his wife, Karen, and two children – Colin, a sophomore at Piedmont High, and Molly, a seventh grader at Piedmont Middle School. “The past few years took a lot out of all of us, and I’m lucky to be able to take a break,” Tulloch said. “I’m certainly not leaving the community, and this is definitely not a retirement. I love this city, and I want to continue to help it grow. The possibility that I’ll return to City Hall is absolutely there, but I don’t know right now what form that would take. I will always be proud of the work I’ve done here.” The City has engaged Bob Murray & Associates, an executive recruiting firm, to conduct a nationwide search for a new permanent City Clerk. On the firm’s website, the filing deadline is shown to be August 20, 2023. Until a permanent replacement is hired, the City Council has appointed Sheri Hartz to serve as interim City Clerk in Piedmont, effective after Tulloch’s departure on August 4. Hartz served as the City Clerk of Novato from 2010 to 2016, and as City Clerk of Emeryville from 2016 to 2022, when she retired. After two sessions of ransacking the store, the suspects stole an estimated $100,000 in merchandise and money. Based upon surveillance photos, after one ten-minute session ransacking the business for valuable merchandise, the suspects left, and briefly parked at Safeway. When no alarm or alert was heard, they returned to enter the building again to the back of the building and spent 25 minutes stealing items. According to Ace Hardware Manager Shaun Braga it was the second stint of burglary that resulted in the biggest loses. Power tools and cash were taken, and items were strewn all around the store and parking lot. A door on the side of the building was pried open and bolt cutters were used to cut a padlock. Piedmont police found the bolt cutter left behind. Surveillance video showed one of the three suspect vehicles leaving the city two hours later, at 6:17 a.m. Police Dispatch was notified of the loss at 8:40 a.m. Grand Ace Hardware, which has been in business for 50 years, has hired a security guard since the robbery. Moreover, the trail on the right provided an unforgettable walk with bushels of wildflowers lining the path and butterflies fluttering around unbothered around you. Off to your right will be the magnificent Granite Chief Mountain and the Desolation Wilderness. From Washeshu Peak, hikers get a clear view of Lake Tahoe and get a glimpse of Five Lakes while panning to the right—which is a The view of Granite Chief from the peak near the Watson Monument. The Watson Emigrant Pass Marker is an original trail marker for the Placer County Emigrant Road. trail we covered in September of last year. Pack a lunch to eat with the view. There are also mounds of shale enclosures to protect from the wind if needed. Returning to High Camp from Washeshu Peak will round out your day at four miles. However, those interested can hang a left at the Gold Coast Express ski lift to take the route up to the Watson Monument Emigrant Pass Marker. Walking to the marker adds .4 miles to your day and another 300 feet in elevation gain, while the nearby peak to the left of the marker (when facing the plaque) gives an even closer look of Granite Chief. Trails which led to the Granite Chief Wilderness were closed for maintenance. The Watson Monument marks the former Placer County Emigrant Road. It reads an inscription: “The Placer County Emigrant Road, known today as the Western States Trail, extended from Yankee Jim’s on the Foresthill divide to the Washoe Valley in Nevada. Built in 1852, the road served emigrants before providing a link to the Comstock boom towns such as Gold Hill, Silver City and Virginia City in Nevada. In September 1931, pioneer horseman Robert Montgomery Watson, along with the Native Sons of the Golden West, completed marking the portion of the trail from Lake Tahoe to Auburn. The granite monument before you is the original trail marker constructed by Robert Montgomery Watson during the summer of 1931.” Finish your six mile day with a bite to eat at High Camp before traveling back down. Those interested can take the Shirley Canyon Trail if they’d rather descend by foot. The aerial tram ride to-andfrom is $30. Foot traffic was seldom on a Monday at noon with just 18 people on the trail. However, you can expect a crammed tram-ride reminiscent of a Monday-morning on BART. For more information at things to do at Palisades Tahoe and High Camp, visit www.PalisadesTahoe. com. This article updates information in a column published in the Post in August 2021.
